cf.title: Tighten SCRAM iteration parsing and bound libpq PBKDF2 work

input.subject: Tighten SCRAM iteration parsing and bound libpq PBKDF2 work

verdict_reasoning: The parsing fix and the connect_timeout check have reviewer support in message #2, but three design points are open. The default cap of 100000 rejects servers that the scram_iterations setting allows (standards-compat-1), and the cap overlaps with connect_timeout once 0003-0005 land (already-exists-1). The shape of the interrupt hook in src/common is unsettled (maintenance-fit-2). All are fixable, and 0006 can be dropped or made opt-in without harm to the rest.

brief.title: Strict SCRAM iteration parsing and bounded client-side PBKDF2 work in libpq
brief.problem: The backend and libpq parse the SCRAM iteration count with strtol() into a long and store it in an int, so values above INT_MAX truncate and zero or negative counts pass. Separately, a server can advertise a huge iteration count and keep a libpq client in PBKDF2 past connect_timeout. This affects services that connect to user-supplied database hosts.
brief.proposed_design: A new helper in src/common, scram_parse_iterations(), accepts only decimal digits in 1..INT_MAX, and both parsers use it. libpq copies the blocking connect deadline into PGconn, and the shared PBKDF2 loop calls an optional interrupt callback that aborts once that deadline passes. A new libpq option, scram_max_iterations (default 100000, 0 disables), rejects larger server counts before any PBKDF2 work starts.
user_visible_surface: New libpq connection parameter scram_max_iterations and environment variable PGSCRAMMAXITERATIONS, default 100000.
connect_timeout now also bounds SCRAM PBKDF2 work on the blocking path, with a new "connection timeout expired" error during authentication.
New C function scram_SaltedPasswordExt() in src/common, which takes an interrupt callback; scram_SaltedPassword() keeps its signature.
The backend rejects stored SCRAM secrets whose iteration count is zero, negative, non-decimal or above INT_MAX.
New test module src/test/modules/test_scram with an SQL wrapper around scram_parse_iterations().
author_claims: A stored secret with 2147483648 iterations, set through ALTER USER, overflows to -1 and skips the empty-password check.
With a 10M iteration count and connect_timeout=1, psql took about 12.7 s before; it fails at once with the cap and after about 1 s with the cap disabled.
pgjdbc and node-postgres ship a similar limit with a 100K default.
The security list judged the client-side denial of service out of scope as a security issue.
The truncation does not allow logins without the password.
brief.thread_state: Daniel Gustafsson supports honoring connect_timeout during SCRAM but objects to frontend-only parameters in shared code and to passing PGconn to a callback. He is -1 on the new connection parameter and questions the 4096-iteration check interval; the author's reply has no response yet.
unclear: The thread does not say which patches, if any, should be backpatched; the author asks.
Async PQconnectPoll() callers get no timeout protection, and the proposal has no plan for them.
The proposal does not say what a frontend equivalent of CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() would look like, as Gustafsson requests.
No check interval is settled; the author floats 256 in place of 4096.
The thread has no data on how many deployments use scram_iterations above 100000 and would break on upgrade.
The 1-second TAP test is timing-sensitive, and no reviewer has commented on it.

prior_attempts.title: timeout parameters in libpq
prior_attempts.quote: I'd like clarifications about the use case that needs this specific feature, especially to understand why the server-side "statement_timeout" setting is not right enough.
prior_attempts.reason: Fabien COELHO's review asked why the server-side statement_timeout is not enough for socket_timeout. He also found that a timeout drops and resets the connection instead of cancelling the query, and that pqWait duplicates pqWaitTimed logic. The patch had no tests and no documentation. Andrei Yahorau warned that the pqWait change breaks callers that expect to wait forever; the author planned new patches after an absence, and the visible thread ends with the review.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P5 added new libpq timeout parameters for query and network waits. This proposal extends the existing connect_timeout to PBKDF2 work and adds an iteration cap, and message #3 gives a use case.

objections.title: Default scram_max_iterations of 100000 breaks existing high-iteration servers
objections.failure_scenario: A site runs the server with scram_iterations = 500000, which the GUC allows. After a client-package upgrade, psql, pg_dump, postgres_fdw, dblink and a standby's walreceiver all fail with "exceeding scram_max_iterations". The site learns of it at the first reconnect after the upgrade, which may be a replication reconnect during an incident.
objections.argument: Message #1 says deployments with scram_iterations of 250K to 1M exist and would need the parameter set on libpq upgrade. Raising the iteration count is the documented way to harden stored secrets, so the users hit are the ones who followed that advice. Every libpq-based tool and each primary_conninfo or user mapping would need the new option. Gustafsson (message #2) is -1 on the parameter and warns that a wrong value rejects connections in error; message #3 answers with driver precedent, which does not cover this upgrade path.
objections.author_must_show: Why should the default reject servers that use iteration counts the scram_iterations GUC accepts, instead of 0 with connect_timeout as the default protection?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 itself says deployments with scram_iterations of 250K to 1M exist and would need the parameter set on libpq upgrade. The thread has no answer to Gustafsson's point that a wrong value rejects valid connections, and a default of 0 would avoid the break.

objections.title: The PBKDF2 interrupt hook is shaped for libpq, not shared code
objections.failure_scenario: src/common gains scram_SaltedPasswordExt(), a callback that receives a PGconn, and a frontend-only check interval. Later, another auth method or a frontend tool that derives SCRAM secrets needs a similar abort. It has to copy this pattern or change the signature again, and the old shim stays.
objections.argument: Message #2 objects to frontend-only parameters in code shared with the backend and to passing the whole PGconn, and it asks for something closer to CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS(). Message #3 asks whether a frontend example exists and offers to have the backend pass a CFI wrapper, but the design is not settled. Two entry points, scram_SaltedPassword() and scram_SaltedPasswordExt(), would then live in src/common indefinitely.
objections.author_must_show: What frontend interrupt mechanism, used the same way by backend and frontend callers, would replace the PGconn callback and the Ext shim?

critic.reasoning: Gustafsson raised both points in message #2, and message #3 answers with a question and two alternatives. The thread settles neither the callback shape nor the Ext shim, so the internal API is still open.

objections.title: Stricter secret parsing changes how existing role passwords are classified
objections.failure_scenario: A role has a stored secret such as 'SCRAM-SHA-256$+4096:...' or one with an out-of-range count, which strtol() accepted. pg_dumpall emits it, and the patched server restores it. If the parse fails, the server may store the whole string as a new plaintext password and hash it, so the old password stops working without any error.
objections.argument: 0001 makes the backend reject leading signs, whitespace, zero and values above INT_MAX in stored secrets. The server classifies a password string by whether it parses as a SCRAM secret, so a stricter parser can change what CREATE ROLE ... PASSWORD and ALTER ROLE do with existing dump output. Message #1 calls this a behavior change and still asks whether to backpatch it. The proposal does not say how existing pg_authid rows and dumped secrets are treated.
objections.author_must_show: After 0001, what does CREATE ROLE ... PASSWORD do with a previously accepted secret that the new parser rejects, and should it raise an error instead of storing a plaintext password?

critic.reasoning: The backend treats a string that fails parse_scram_secret() as a plaintext password, so create role or alter role hashes it on restore. A hand-written secret such as '$+4096:' works today and would stop working without an error. Such secrets are rare, so fixable.

objections.title: scram_max_iterations overlaps with connect_timeout once 0003-0005 land
objections.failure_scenario: A site runs scram_iterations at 500000 and upgrades libpq. Every client that has not set scram_max_iterations now fails to connect with the new error, even though connect_timeout, after 0003-0005, already bounds the PBKDF2 work for blocking clients that set a timeout.
objections.argument: With patches 0003-0005, connect_timeout bounds PBKDF2 on the blocking path, so for those clients the cap adds a second limit on the same work. The author's answer in message #1 is that the cap also covers clients with no timeout and async PQconnectPoll() callers. Clients without a timeout can set connect_timeout today, and async callers might be served by a deadline taken at PQconnectStart(). Message #2 is -1 on another niche connection parameter, and message #3 does not answer that point.
objections.author_must_show: Why can async PQconnectPoll() callers not be protected by extending connect_timeout or a connect-start deadline, instead of adding a separate parameter with a default that rejects existing high-iteration setups?

critic.reasoning: Once 0003-0005 land, the cap adds protection only for callers without a timeout and for async callers. The thread does not show that this gap justifies a permanent parameter, and Gustafsson's -1 on it has no reply on that point.

refuted.title: Stricter secret parsing may turn existing pg_authid entries into plaintext passwords
refuted.failure_scenario: A cluster holds a role secret like 'SCRAM-SHA-256$2147483648:...' or '$0:...', set through ALTER USER as message #3 shows. After a minor update or pg_upgrade, the new parser rejects it. get_password_type() then likely classifies the string as plaintext, so the literal secret string becomes a working password for anyone who has read it from a backup.
refuted.argument: Patch 0001 changes which rolpassword values the backend accepts as SCRAM secrets, and message #1 asks whether to backpatch it. In Postgres a string that fails parse_scram_secret() is treated as a plaintext password, both at login and when pg_dumpall output is restored by CREATE ROLE during pg_upgrade. Message #3 shows such rows can be created today. The proposal does not say what happens to existing rows that hold them.
refuted.author_must_show: How are existing pg_authid secrets with out-of-range iteration counts handled after a minor update, dump/restore or pg_upgrade, so they are not reinterpreted as plaintext passwords?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2 for the dump and restore path. The login claim is incorrect: the server never accepts a stored value as a plaintext password, so an existing row that fails the parse makes authentication fail.

refuted.title: Default 100000 cap rejects valid server-first-messages from existing servers
refuted.failure_scenario: A site runs a server with scram_iterations = 500000, which is valid since that setting accepts 1..INT_MAX. A distribution update ships the new libpq, and every psql and libpq-based application then fails at connect with "exceeding scram_max_iterations". The site learns of it only after the client upgrade, with no server-side change.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says deployments with scram_iterations of 250K to 1M exist and would need to set the parameter on libpq upgrade. That makes a server message that conforms to the protocol fail depending on the client version, which is a cross-version compatibility break. In message #2, Gustafsson is -1 on the parameter because a wrong value rejects connections, and the thread has no reply to that point. The connect_timeout check already bounds the blocking path without rejecting valid servers.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should a default libpq release reject servers configured within the documented scram_iterations range, and not ship with the cap at 0?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. It describes the same upgrade break for a server with scram_iterations = 500000 and asks the same question about a default of 0.

refuted.title: Default cap of 100000 penalizes servers that chose stronger SCRAM hashing
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator raised scram_iterations to 500000 to make stolen pg_authid hashes harder to crack. After a libpq upgrade, psql and every libpq-based driver refuse to connect. The quick fix is setting PGSCRAMMAXITERATIONS=0 everywhere, which removes the protection, or lowering scram_iterations, which weakens stored secrets.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says deployments with scram_iterations in the 250K to 1M range exist and would need to set the parameter on upgrade. The default turns stronger server-side password hashing into a connection failure, so it pushes operators toward weaker hashing or a global opt-out. Message #2 notes that a wrong setting rejects connections in error. pgjdbc and node-postgres using 100K shows other drivers chose it, but no thread message shows how many libpq users run above that value.
refuted.author_must_show: How many deployments run scram_iterations above 100000, and why is a nonzero default better for them than an opt-in cap plus the connect_timeout check?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The added point that operators may lower scram_iterations or disable the cap everywhere is a consequence of the same default.

refuted.title: Attacker who supplies the connection string can disable both protections
refuted.failure_scenario: A reporting service accepts a full connection URI from its users. An attacker submits a URI pointing at a hostile server, with scram_max_iterations=0 and no connect_timeout. The service's connection thread spins in PBKDF2 as it does today, and the operator learns this only from CPU alerts.
refuted.argument: Message #3 gives the motivating case as a service that connects to user-specified databases. Patch 0006 makes the cap an ordinary connection option, so whoever writes the connection string can turn it off. The proposed libpq.sgml text does not tell applications that they must override scram_max_iterations and connect_timeout after the user's URI is expanded. Without that, the cap only protects services that accept a bare host and port.
refuted.author_must_show: How should an application that accepts user-supplied URIs force scram_max_iterations and connect_timeout, and will the documentation say so?

critic.reasoning: The scenario ends in the behaviour libpq has today, so the patch does not make it worse. An application that passes a full user-written URI to libpq must already override options such as connect_timeout, and the missing documentation sentence is outside levels 1-2.

refuted.title: scram_max_iterations adds a permanent option with a breaking default
refuted.failure_scenario: A site runs scram_iterations = 500000 and upgrades libpq through a distribution package. Every client, including psql and pg_dump, then fails with "exceeding scram_max_iterations (100000)". The site finds out at the first connection after the upgrade and must set PGSCRAMMAXITERATIONS=0 everywhere.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says deployments with scram_iterations in the 250K to 1M range exist, and the thread has no count of them. Message #2 is -1 on another connection parameter, because no one can document a correct value and a wrong value rejects valid connections. Once the option ships, libpq must keep it in connection strings, URIs and the environment for good. The use case in message #3 is services that connect to hosts chosen by their users, and connect_timeout from 0004 already covers most of it.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is connect_timeout during PBKDF2 not enough for hosted services, and what would justify a default other than 0, given that 0 changes nothing on upgrade?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1 for the breaking default and of already-exists-1 for the overlap with connect_timeout. It adds no separate failure.

refuted.title: Deadline on PGconn makes connect_timeout depend on the connection path
refuted.failure_scenario: An application that drives PQconnectPoll() sets connect_timeout and expects the same protection as PQconnectdb(). Its connect_deadline is never set, so a server that advertises a huge iteration count still pins it. Any future auth path that should honour the deadline must remember to read connect_deadline, and nothing fails if it does not.
refuted.argument: The 0004 commit message says async callers never have connect_deadline set, and message #1 justifies putting it on PGconn so GSSAPI or LDAP paths "might want to consult" it. That leaves a per-auth-method duty with no enforcement. connect_timeout would also mean different things on the blocking and async paths, and the documentation hunk only names the blocking path.
refuted.author_must_show: How will async PQconnectPoll() users and future auth methods get the same deadline behaviour without each code path having to remember to check it?

critic.reasoning: libpq applies connect_timeout only in the blocking connect path today, and PQconnectPoll() callers run their own timeouts. The patch follows that existing split and states it, and the duty on future auth methods is speculative.

refuted.title: Default scram_max_iterations of 100000 makes users who never opted in pay
refuted.failure_scenario: A site runs scram_iterations = 500000 for stronger password hashing and upgrades libpq through its distribution. Every psql, pg_dump and application connection then fails with "exceeding scram_max_iterations (100000)". The site finds out at upgrade time and must set PGSCRAMMAXITERATIONS on every client.
refuted.argument: The benefit goes to services that connect to user-supplied hosts, but the default moves the cost to every site that followed the advice to raise scram_iterations. Message #1 says deployments in the 250K to 1M range exist, and the thread has no estimate of how many there are. Message #2 warns that a wrong setting means "rejecting connections in err". A default of 0 would keep the cost with the feature's users.
refuted.author_must_show: How many deployments run scram_iterations above 100000, and why should they reconfigure clients so that hosted platforms get protection by default?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The who-pays argument is the same default-of-100000 break, with the same proposed remedy of a default of 0.

refuted.title: Demand for scram_max_iterations rests on one class of application
refuted.failure_scenario: The project adds a permanent connection parameter and environment variable for multi-tenant services that connect to untrusted hosts. Most libpq users never meet a hostile server, and for them it is one more option to understand. Once connect_timeout bounds PBKDF2, the remaining gap is async callers and callers without a timeout.
refuted.argument: The only use case in the thread is a SaaS or reporting tool that connects to user-specified databases (message #3). pgjdbc and node-postgres had a stronger reason, because their PBKDF2 could not be interrupted at all. Once 0003-0005 land, libpq would not have that problem on the blocking path. Message #2 is -1 on the parameter as a niche case, and no other user or report asks for it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which libpq users, other than services connecting to untrusted hosts, would need scram_max_iterations once connect_timeout bounds PBKDF2 work?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which states the same narrow remaining gap after 0003-0005. The material also shows some demand, since pgjdbc and node-postgres ship the same limit.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: 0001 changes which stored rolpassword values the backend accepts as SCRAM secrets.

touch_points.label: wire protocol
touch_points.reason: libpq parses the server-first-message more strictly and, with 0006, rejects iteration counts above the cap.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: 0004 adds scram_SaltedPasswordExt() with an interrupt callback to src/common; 0003 adds a field to PGconn.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: 0006 adds the libpq option scram_max_iterations and the environment variable PGSCRAMMAXITERATIONS.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: A dumped secret that strtol() accepted and the new parser rejects may restore differently.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The series changes SCRAM secret validation and client behaviour against a hostile server.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Message #1 asks whether 0001 and 0003-0005 should be backpatched; 0001 is a behavior change.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A permanent connection option, an environment variable and a second PBKDF2 entry point in src/common.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: 0004 adds a periodic callback check inside the PBKDF2 loop that every SCRAM login runs in libpq.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: After 0003-0005, scram_max_iterations bounds the same work that connect_timeout already bounds on the blocking path.

questions: Why can async PQconnectPoll() callers not be protected by a deadline taken at connection start, instead of a separate scram_max_iterations parameter?
If scram_max_iterations stays, why should its default reject servers whose scram_iterations is within the allowed range, instead of defaulting to 0?
What frontend interrupt mechanism, used the same way by backend and frontend callers, would replace the PGconn callback and the scram_SaltedPasswordExt() shim?
After 0001, what does CREATE ROLE ... PASSWORD do with a previously accepted secret that the new parser rejects: raise an error, or store it as a plaintext password?
Which of 0001 and 0003-0005 do you propose to backpatch, given that 0001 rejects stored secrets that current branches accept?

committability.owner_note: Daniel Gustafsson reviewed in message #2 and shows knowledge of the SCRAM iteration design. The owner must know libpq connection setup and the shared SCRAM code in src/common.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a stricter stored-secret parser on every branch that gets 0001, a new interrupt API in src/common, and, if 0006 goes in, a connection option and default that libpq must keep for good.
committability.author_follow_up: The author replied within a day with a reproduction (message #3), moved the entry to the next CommitFest in October, and says he added similar limits to pgjdbc and node-postgres.

priority.reason: The timeout protection serves services that connect to user-supplied hosts (message #3), and the parsing fix is hygiene that the reviewer supports. Six small patches touch libpq authentication and src/common, and the reviewer's points from message #2 on the hook shape and the parameter are still open.

provisional_note: The code was not read. Not judged: what the backend does when the new parser rejects a stored secret, how connect_deadline is reset per host, and whether the 1-second TAP test is stable.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Channel binding support for SCRAM-SHA-256
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds SCRAM channel binding (SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS) over SSL connections, using tls-unique from the OpenSSL TLS Finished message and, in a later patch, tls-server-end-point from a hash of the server certificate. It also adds libpq connection parameters saslname and saslchannelbinding so the client can force the mechanism and binding type, plus SSL tests.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut's review found the client-side channel binding negotiation wrong: the client sent "y" whenever SSL was compiled in but unused, and never sent "y" when the server did not advertise SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS. He also objected that the server rejected "n" clients on all SSL connections, and that the tls-server-end-point hash selection did not follow RFC 5929. The design of the libpq connection parameters was still under discussion, so the author returned the patch with feedback for rework.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think the channel-binding negotiation on the client side is wrong.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support for SCRAM-SHA-256
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch series adds SCRAM-SHA-256 password authentication over a SASL exchange, with SCRAM verifiers stored in pg_authid.rolpassword and password_encryption turned into an enum that accepts 'scram'. It also moves SHA and encoding routines to src/common and adds a PASSWORD val USING protocol clause to CREATE/ALTER ROLE.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author marked the entry returned with feedback himself, after review by Heikki Linnakangas produced a list of required changes. The list: use the base64 canonical form without whitespace that the SCRAM spec requires, move only sha2.c and base64 to src/common, replace random() in libpq with a proper random source, send RFC 5802 e= error messages, and drop the md5-or-scram option in pg_hba.conf. The password_encryption enum patch from the series was committed separately.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: random() called in the client is no good. We need something better here.

precedents_retrieved.title: Authorization facility for multiple password verifiers + SCRAM-SHA1
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace pg_authid.rolpassword with a new catalog, pg_auth_verifiers, that stores several password verifiers per role (plain, md5, later SCRAM), with a PASSWORD VERIFIERS option for CREATE/ALTER ROLE, a list-valued password_encryption and a reworked password check hook. Later patches in the series add SASL messages to the protocol and SCRAM-SHA-1 authentication on top of that catalog.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author, Michael Paquier, returned the patch himself because nobody answered his November proposal for an allowed_password_verifiers GUC and a cleanup function. Robert Haas questioned the need for multiple verifiers per role, but his messages appear only as quoted fragments.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I am going to mark this patch as returned with feedback because of a visible lack of interest.

precedents_retrieved.title: de-TOAST'ing using a iterator
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an iterator that de-TOASTs and decompresses a toasted value piece by piece, so callers fetch only the part they need. The first user is position(), which can stop early when the match is near the start of the value.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stalled with design problems still open. The iterator structs are exposed in headers, detoast.h ends up including genam.h, and the TOAST code may become heapam-dependent again. John Naylor, who had taken the patch over, said he could not fix the architectural awkwardness and would not work on it in the near future. Anastasia Lubennikova then returned it with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
For background, this was a 2019 GSoC project where
I was reviewer of record, and the patch is mostly good, but there is some
architectural awkwardness. I have tried to address that, but have not had
success.

precedents_retrieved.title: timeout parameters in libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patches add a tcp_user_timeout parameter on the server and in libpq that sets the Linux TCP_USER_TIMEOUT socket option. They also add a libpq socket_timeout parameter that closes the connection when a query result does not arrive in time.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Fabien COELHO's review asked why the server-side statement_timeout is not enough for socket_timeout. He also found that a timeout drops and resets the connection instead of cancelling the query, and that pqWait duplicates pqWaitTimed logic. The patch had no tests and no documentation. Andrei Yahorau warned that the pqWait change breaks callers that expect to wait forever; the author planned new patches after an absence, and the visible thread ends with the review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I'd like clarifications about the use case that needs this specific feature, especially to understand why the server-side "statement_timeout" setting is not right enough.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support for SCRAM-SHA-256
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Noah Misch, Peter Eisentraut, Michael Paquier
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds SCRAM-SHA-256 password authentication to Postgres, with supporting refactoring that moves SHA and encoding routines to src/common. Early versions also added a pg_auth_verifiers catalog and a password_protocols setting for password protocol aging; later work focused on SCRAM verifiers stored in pg_authid.rolpassword.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author marked it returned with feedback because key design decisions were still open. There was no agreement on how to implement SASLprep normalization of passwords (libidn under the LGPL, or an in-core Unicode table). Reviewers also questioned the pg_hba.conf keyword "scram" as not future-proof, and no one agreed on the "plain:" prefix for plaintext passwords in rolpassword.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With decisions on this matter pending, I am marking this patch as
"returned with feedback".

precedents_retrieved.title: Iterating on IndexTuple attributes and nbtree page-level dynamic prefix truncation
precedents_retrieved.summary: Patch 0001 adds an API to iterate over index tuple attributes and reuse the offset of the last extracted attribute, so extracting all attributes costs O(n) instead of O(n*n) when attcacheoff cannot be used. Patch 0002 uses this to truncate attribute prefixes dynamically during nbtree binary search within a page, as a first step toward prefix truncation in nbtree.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author's own June 2021 benchmarks showed regressions in multi-column indexes that can use attcacheoff: about 2% for insert and 15% for reindex with both patches. The author said this had to be fixed before commit, but no fixed version appears in the thread. In December 2021 Daniel Gustafsson moved the entry forward and noted that the patch no longer applied and needed a rebase. The visible messages do not show a rebased version or the final decision.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Evidently, this needs improvements in the (likely common) attcacheoff-enabled multi-column case; as I don't think we can reasonably commit a 10+% regression.

precedents_retrieved.title: User functions for building SCRAM secrets
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Daniel Gustafsson, Michael Paquier, Magnus Hagander
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a SQL function, scram_build_secret_sha256, that builds a SCRAM-SHA-256 secret from a plaintext password, with an optional salt and iteration count. Its purpose is a SQL equivalent of the hashing done for CREATE/ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD, for uses such as password history checks and precomputing secrets for a remote server.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected that the function requires sending the plaintext password to the server, where it can end up in logs, and SCRAM was meant to avoid that. They suggested other directions: more flexible \password and libpq, GUCs for SCRAM parameters, or a predefined role for changing one's own password. They also questioned allowing a user-chosen salt or low iteration counts. The discussion did not reach consensus, and the entry was returned with feedback after about eight months without activity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Allowing scram_build_secret_sha256('password', 'a', 1); with the password potentially going in cleartext over the wire and into the logs doesn't seem like a great tradeoff for the (IMHO) niche usecases it would satisfy.

precedents_retrieved.title: iteration over record in plpgsql
precedents_retrieved.summary:

This reverts commit 728f86fec65537eade8d9e751961782ddb527934.

The signal handling was a few bricks shy of a load in that commit,
which made the walreceiver non-responsive to SIGTERM while it was
waiting for the connection to be established. That prevented a standby
from being promoted.

Since it was non-essential refactoring, let's revert it to make v16
work the same as earlier releases. I reverted it in 'master' too, to
keep the branches in sync. The refactoring was a good idea as such,
but it needs a bit more work. Once we have developed a complete patch
with this issue fixed, let's re-apply that to 'master'.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent proposed the same idea. P5 only asked why an existing setting was not enough, and message #3 gives a use case and explains why connect_timeout alone does not cover clients without a timeout or async callers. P22 has no recorded reason. The thread mentions a security-list report and similar pgjdbc and node-postgres limits (message #3), but no earlier pgsql-hackers attempt.
The connect_timeout change (0003-0005) adds no user-facing syntax and only makes an existing timeout cover more work, so it raises no compatibility objection from this angle.
There are no WAL, replication, on-disk heap or index changes. The PGconn field is in libpq-int.h and scram_SaltedPassword() keeps its signature, so I see no ABI break.
Patch 0001, the parsing fix, closes a real gap: per message #3, an overflowing iteration count skips the empty-password check. From the security angle, 0001 needs no objection.
The parsing fix in 0001 and the test module in 0002 raise no maintenance or fit concern from this angle.
Nothing in Postgres caps the server-advertised iteration count today, and 0001 and 0003-0005 fix or extend existing mechanisms, so this angle raises nothing against them.
The parsing fix (0001) and honoring connect_timeout during SCRAM (0003-0005) have reviewer support in message #2, so this review raises no demand objection against them.
